t: Every house in Hollow Fen burns two lamps.
Light a third, and the Moth takes the house.
Not the people inside. The whole house.
In the morning, there's only a square of clean dirt.
Twelve squares so far. We walk around them.
I trim the wicks on our street.
Every evening, old Wren walks by and counts our windows.
One. Two. Then she taps her cane twice and moves on.
We eat by two lamps. We read by two lamps. We get married by two lamps.
Nobody has ever seen the Moth land.
You only see the dust.
It falls first, like gold snow. Then the wind comes from above.
Its wings are wider than the church.
And on the wings, two huge eyes that never blink, because they're painted on.
My little sister Pell hates the dark.
She says two lamps leave the corners hungry.
Last winter, the Brannocks had a birthday.
One candle on a cake. Just one.
That made three.
The dust started falling during the song.
I watched from our window, with my hand over Pell's eyes.
The roof lifted off like a lid.
Then the walls. Then the porch. Then the cake, still lit.
No screaming. Just the song, getting smaller, going up.
In the morning, Wren raked the square of dirt where they used to live.
She painted new words on the well. Two lamps. Always.
Nobody bought candles that year. Nobody sang.
Even the church kept its two lamps. Not one more.
Pell stopped talking about the dark after that.
Then, three nights ago, she started smiling at bedtime.
Tonight, I found out why.
Under her blanket, there's a jar.
Inside the jar, forty fireflies.
Forty little lights, blinking on and off, on and off.
The dust is already falling on our roof.
Gold on our roof, on our door, on my sister's window.
Outside, Wren is counting our windows. One. Two. Forty-two.
Then she stops counting.
Wren never stops counting.
Pell won't let go of the jar. She just whispers, mine.
So I take both our lamps off the hooks.
I light every candle in the kitchen drawer.
I tie them to my coat, my belt, my boots.
I'm the brightest thing in Hollow Fen.
Brighter than the jar. Brighter than a birthday.
I open the door and run, past the well, into the marsh.
Behind me, every window in town goes dark.
Nobody wants to be the brightest house tonight.
Above me, the wind is coming down.
The reeds lie flat. The candles lean, but they stay lit.
My whole life, I counted to two.
Tonight, I'm the third lamp.
